L57: /*
L58:  * Structures for the extended file attribute retrieval system call
L59:  * (statx()).
L60:  *
L61:  * The caller passes a mask of what they're specifically interested in as a
L62:  * parameter to statx().  What statx() actually got will be indicated in
L63:  * st_mask upon return.
L64:  *
L65:  * For each bit in the mask argument:
L66:  *
L67:  * - if the datum is not supported:
L68:  *
L69:  *   - the bit will be cleared, and
L70:  *
L71:  *   - the datum will be set to an appropriate fabricated value if one is
L72:  *     available (eg. CIFS can take a default uid and gid), otherwise
L73:  *
L74:  *   - the field will be cleared;
L75:  *
L76:  * - otherwise, if explicitly requested:
L77:  *
L78:  *   - the datum will be synchronised to the server if AT_STATX_FORCE_SYNC is
L79:  *     set or if the datum is considered out of date, and
L80:  *
L81:  *   - the field will be filled in and the bit will be set;
L82:  *
L83:  * - otherwise, if not requested, but available in approximate form without any
L84:  *   effort, it will be filled in anyway, and the bit will be set upon return
L85:  *   (it might not be up to date, however, and no attempt will be made to
L86:  *   synchronise the internal state first);
L87:  *
L88:  * - otherwise the field and the bit will be cleared before returning.
L89:  *
L90:  * Items in STATX_BASIC_STATS may be marked unavailable on return, but they
L91:  * will have values installed for compatibility purposes so that stat() and
L92:  * co. can be emulated in userspace.
L93:  */
L94: struct statx {
L95: 	/* 0x00 */
L96: 	__u32	stx_mask;	/* What results were written [uncond] */
L97: 	__u32	stx_blksize;	/* Preferred general I/O size [uncond] */
L98: 	__u64	stx_attributes;	/* Flags conveying information about the file [uncond] */
L99: 	/* 0x10 */
L100: 	__u32	stx_nlink;	/* Number of hard links */
L101: 	__u32	stx_uid;	/* User ID of owner */
L102: 	__u32	stx_gid;	/* Group ID of owner */
L103: 	__u16	stx_mode;	/* File mode */
L104: 	__u16	__spare0[1];
L105: 	/* 0x20 */
L106: 	__u64	stx_ino;	/* Inode number */
L107: 	__u64	stx_size;	/* File size */
L108: 	__u64	stx_blocks;	/* Number of 512-byte blocks allocated */
L109: 	__u64	stx_attributes_mask; /* Mask to show what's supported in stx_attributes */
L110: 	/* 0x40 */
L111: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_atime;	/* Last access time */
L112: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_btime;	/* File creation time */
L113: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_ctime;	/* Last attribute change time */
L114: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_mtime;	/* Last data modification time */
L115: 	/* 0x80 */
L116: 	__u32	stx_rdev_major;	/* Device ID of special file [if bdev/cdev] */
L117: 	__u32	stx_rdev_minor;
L118: 	__u32	stx_dev_major;	/* ID of device containing file [uncond] */
L119: 	__u32	stx_dev_minor;
L120: 	/* 0x90 */
L121: 	__u64	stx_mnt_id;
L122: 	__u32	stx_dio_mem_align;	/* Memory buffer alignment for direct I/O */
L123: 	__u32	stx_dio_offset_align;	/* File offset alignment for direct I/O */
L124: 	/* 0xa0 */
L125: 	__u64	__spare3[12];	/* Spare space for future expansion */
L126: 	/* 0x100 */
L127: };

L174:  */

L176: #define STATX_ATTR_IMMUTABLE		0x00000010 /* [I] File is marked immutable */
L177: #define STATX_ATTR_APPEND		0x00000020 /* [I] File is append-only */
L178: #define STATX_ATTR_NODUMP		0x00000040 /* [I] File is not to be dumped */
L179: #define STATX_ATTR_ENCRYPTED		0x00000800 /* [I] File requires key to decrypt in fs */
L180: #define STATX_ATTR_AUTOMOUNT		0x00001000 /* Dir: Automount trigger */
L181: #define STATX_ATTR_MOUNT_ROOT		0x00002000 /* Root of a mount */
L182: #define STATX_ATTR_VERITY		0x00100000 /* [I] Verity protected file */
L183: #define STATX_ATTR_DAX			0x00200000 /* File is currently in DAX state */

L1: # cite0†`os` — Miscellaneous operating system interfacescite0†¶ L2: 
L3: Source code: cite1†Lib/os.py†github.com L4: 
L5: * * *
L6: This module provides a portable way of using operating system dependent functionality. If you just want to read or write a file see cite2†`open()` , if you want to manipulate paths, see the cite3†`os.path` module, and if you want to read all the lines in all the files on the command line see the cite4†`fileinput` module. For creating temporary files and directories see the cite5†`tempfile` module, and for high-level file and directory handling see the cite6†`shutil` module.
L7: Notes on the availability of these functions:
L8: 
L9:   * The design of all built-in operating system dependent modules of Python is such that as long as the same functionality is available, it uses the same interface; for example, the function `os.stat(path)` returns stat information about path in the same format (which happens to have originated with the POSIX interface).
L10:   * Extensions peculiar to a particular operating system are also available through the cite0†`os` module, but using them is of course a threat to portability.
L11: 
L12:   * All functions accepting path or file names accept both bytes and string objects, and result in an object of the same type, if a path or file name is returned.
L13: 
L14:   * On VxWorks, os.popen, os.fork, os.execv and os.spawn*p* are not supported.
L15: 
L16: Note
L17: All functions in this module raise cite7†`OSError` (or subclasses thereof) in the case of invalid or inaccessible file names and paths, or other arguments that have the correct type, but are not accepted by the operating system.
L18: 
L19: exception `os.``error`cite8†¶ L20: 
L21: 
L22: An alias for the built-in cite7†`OSError` exception.
L23: 
L24: `os.``name`cite9†¶ L25: 
L26: 
L27: The name of the operating system dependent module imported. The following names have currently been registered: `'posix'`, `'nt'`, `'java'`.
L28: 
L29: See also
L30: cite10†`sys.platform` has a finer granularity. cite11†`os.uname()` gives system-dependent version information.
L31: 
L32: The cite12†`platform` module provides detailed checks for the system’s identity.
L33: ## File Names, Command Line Arguments, and Environment Variablescite13†¶ L34: 
L35: In Python, file names, command line arguments, and environment variables are represented using the string type. On some systems, decoding these strings to and from bytes is necessary before passing them to the operating system. Python uses the cite14†filesystem encoding and error handler to perform this conversion (see cite15†`sys.getfilesystemencoding()` ).
L36: The cite14†filesystem encoding and error handler are configured at Python startup by the `PyConfig_Read()` function: see cite16†`filesystem_encoding` and cite17†`filesystem_errors` members of cite18†`PyConfig` .
L37: Changed in version 3.1: On some systems, conversion using the file system encoding may fail. In this case, Python uses the cite19†surrogateescape encoding error handler , which means that undecodable bytes are replaced by a Unicode character U+DCxx on decoding, and these are again translated to the original byte on encoding.
L38: The cite14†file system encoding must guarantee to successfully decode all bytes below 128. If the file system encoding fails to provide this guarantee, API functions can raise cite20†`UnicodeError` .
L39: 
L40: See also the cite21†locale encoding .
L41: ## Python UTF-8 Modecite22†¶ L42: 
L43: New in version 3.7: See cite23†PEP 540†www.python.org for more details.
L44: 
L45: The Python UTF-8 Mode ignores the cite21†locale encoding and forces the usage of the UTF-8 encoding:
L46: 
L47:   * Use UTF-8 as the cite14†filesystem encoding .
L48: 
L49:   * cite15†`sys.getfilesystemencoding()` returns `'UTF-8'`.
L50: 
L51:   * cite24†`locale.getpreferredencoding()` returns `'UTF-8'` (the do_setlocale argument has no effect).
L52:   * cite25†`sys.stdin` , cite26†`sys.stdout` , and cite27†`sys.stderr` all use UTF-8 as their text encoding, with the `surrogateescape` cite28†error handler being enabled for cite25†`sys.stdin` and cite26†`sys.stdout` (cite27†`sys.stderr` continues to use `backslashreplace` as it does in the default locale-aware mode)
L53: 
L54:   * On Unix, cite29†`os.device_encoding()` returns `'UTF-8'` rather than the device encoding.
L55: Note that the standard stream settings in UTF-8 mode can be overridden by cite30†`PYTHONIOENCODING` (just as they can be in the default locale-aware mode).
L56: 
L57: As a consequence of the changes in those lower level APIs, other higher level APIs also exhibit different default behaviours:
L58: 
L59:   * Command line arguments, environment variables and filenames are decoded to text using the UTF-8 encoding.
L60: 
L61:   * cite31†`os.fsdecode()` and cite32†`os.fsencode()` use the UTF-8 encoding.
L62:   * cite2†`open()` , cite33†`io.open()` , and cite34†`codecs.open()` use the UTF-8 encoding by default. However, they still use the strict error handler by default so that attempting to open a binary file in text mode is likely to raise an exception rather than producing nonsense data.
L63: 
L64: The cite35†Python UTF-8 Mode is enabled if the LC_CTYPE locale is `C` or `POSIX` at Python startup (see the `PyConfig_Read()` function).
L65: It can be enabled or disabled using the cite36†`-X utf8` command line option and the cite37†`PYTHONUTF8` environment variable.
L66: If the cite37†`PYTHONUTF8` environment variable is not set at all, then the interpreter defaults to using the current locale settings, unless the current locale is identified as a legacy ASCII-based locale (as described for cite38†`PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE` ), and locale coercion is either disabled or fails. In such legacy locales, the interpreter will default to enabling UTF-8 mode unless explicitly instructed not to do so.
L67: The Python UTF-8 Mode can only be enabled at the Python startup. Its value can be read from cite39†`sys.flags.utf8_mode` .
